# The Enemy Within - Developer Diary #21

**The Horned Rat Collector's Edition Covers — Sam Manley & Rachael Macken** 

## **Developer Diary**
## **Enemy Within Campaign – Volume 4: the Horned Rat Collector’s Edition Cover Design**
## **Welcome to Dev Diary 21!**
**In Dev Diary 5,** Cubicle 7 Graphic Designer Rachael Macken discussed her extensive work on the Collector’s Edition covers for Enemy in Shadows — Volume 1 of the Enemy Within Campaign. Rachael, a fan of fantasy art and gaming for years, is currently working across **Warhammer: Age of Sigmar Soulbound** and **Warhammer Fantasy Roleplay.** 

Self-taught digital artist Sam Manley has created numerous amazing pieces of art across multiple lines, including Doctor Who, **Warhammer 40,000 Roleplay: Wrath & Glory** and **Warhammer Fantasy Roleplay.** Back in Dev Diary 4, Sam discussed his creative process and favourite pieces from the **Enemy Within** Campaign, including the _Red Moon_ Inn, a double-page tavern scene. 

In this Diary, Rachael and Sam discuss their creative collaborative process during their creation of the distinctive Collector’s Edition covers for Volume 4, **The Horned Rat.** We think the striking covers really capture WFRP and highlight their extensive research and incredible creative flair. 

Rachael and Sam also created the amazing covers for Volume 2, **Death on the Reik** and Volume 3, **Power Behind the Throne.** 

## **Part 7: the Horned Rat — the Tower**
**Sam:** For this Dev Diary, we’re looking at the striking Limited Edition covers of **The Horned Rat** and T **he Horned Rat Companion** , for the updated Director’s Cut of the **Enemy Within** campaign. 

Before we do, I want to loop right back to the beginning of these covers, and why I was asked to work on them in the first place. I’ve done a little stencil cutting in the past, only ever on a small-ish scale at a few graffiti festivals. Dom McDowall (C7 CEO) was interested in whether that would carry through to a style that would represent something in-world, echoing perhaps a relief-style print that some artists in the Empire may use. Turns out, it carries through very well, especially with the restrictions that come with using this approach. When I’m illustrating in my normal manner, I have effectively unlimited colours and brushstrokes to choose from but with both stencil pieces and these Limited Edition covers, I am restricted to blocks of colour — no blending, no hatching, not really any stippling. Just blocks. I’m also limited with regard to the colours themselves (with stencils, I always preferred to keep my palette very sparse, for reasons of style, cost, and mobility). With this in mind, the scene on each Limited Edition cover has to make sense with only two colours and silver on a black background. The cover has to read properly, be eye-catching, and (and I’m letting out a secret here!) the actual colours of individual elements are _not_ as important as the overall pattern of shapes and colours across the image — this gives me a lot more freedom to think more graphically and less literally. 

The first colour block-in featured brown and green, as you can see in the image above. Talking with Pádraig (WFRP producer), we decided on earthy colours, brown and green, alongside the ever-present white-silver and black. Now, this is where some of that interpretation mentioned earlier comes in, the Doom of Kavzar mentions a white tower, but that didn’t look very good in this format, so silver became the highlight colour. With the very rough block-in approved, I moved on to dropping the lines and cleaning up the colours into cleaner-edged blocks. 

But I wasn’t happy with the brown at all. It wasn’t vibrant enough for this style of work, so I tweaked it to a yellow. The combination of warm-green and mustard-yellow looked appropriately sickly next to one another, so I knew we were on the right track. Very few other changes were made aside from the general refinements of the colours, although I was able to define the mutations on the giant rats a little further. That wrapped up my part of the process, and I handed it over to Rachael to finish it up! 

**Rachael:** Thanks Sam! Really impressive  work. The tower is very well detailed, so I didn’t need to do too much on that apart from the odd shadow and lighting here and there. 

## **Developer Diary**
That’s the history, so let’s dive into the covers themselves! They presented an interesting collection of elements to work with — they were unified by being rat-themed and centred around a tower; contrasted by a feeling of rats in the ascendent in the first, and fleeing in the second. 

So, what’s happening in the image above? Well, this is an interpretation of the Doom of Kavzar (The Curse of Thirteen) — a mythical tale of the origin of the Skaven. A great temple with a bell atop it had been constructed to celebrate the good fortune of the people of the land, but it brought only misery and despair when the bell chimed, as it called forth storms, meteors, and a tide of giant rats that swept across the land. 

The number thirteen is prominent here, as befits anything to do with the hideous ratmen — thirteen rats, thirteen stars, thirteen downard forks of lightning. The clothing of the poor unfortunate men is of a much older style than you’d find in the modern Empire, referencing this being an event that supposedly happened in the long distant past. We see Morrslieb’s skull-face looking down from the skies, and meteors rain down. 

## **Developer Diary**
Rats, specifically huge mutant rats dominate the bottom of the cover. I wanted to tackle adding a wood-grain effect to the giant rats. (I had an idea from block style printing, which I wanted them to look like.) So I researched rats, particularly angry hissing rats — watching images and videos for inspiration. Needless to say, watching these hundreds of massive mutant rats running towards me gave me the absolute shivers. Anyway moving on, using a textured brush, I began removing the solid colour to create a rat-hair like finish. I also added the light and dark hues to give it depth (as in the previous covers). I added quite a bit of detail to the rotting skin around the face and mouth of some rats to add another layer to the horror). 

The poor people that are about to be savagely slaughtered and everything in white, were finished with silver foil. This foil effect needed more separation and shadows so that the foils didn’t merge to become one big blob. I removed parts of the whites to show realistic shadows from the rats. 

The old fifteenth-century wood-framed houses lined in the background are a similar style to  English Tudor houses. I thought this style would work perfectly for this era. I removed the art that was already there. Using inspiration from research and adding the shapes from the illustrator, I created this housing style. Bringing them closer together, back in the day, I’m sure they would be nearly built on top of each other with narrow laneways. 

The comets needed to look more like incredible blazing balls of fire. I used all three tones of light, medium and dark to illustrate the moving flames and ensured the four comets travelled in the same direction. Using different sizes and placing them in different parts of the sky gives a better sense of movement and speed. The comets contrasted against the lightning bolts draws the eye to the horror below. Morr, is a smaller version of the **Enemy in Shadows** cover. Looking down from above as if pulling the strings, gives the image an even creepier effect. 

I wasn’t keen on the two warm colours as they didn’t provide enough contrast. As in previous covers, we used the contrast of hot and cool colours to complement each other. I selected a pantone palette of parrot green (which is a cool green with a hint of blue to give it that heavy colour) and yellow (this bright, warm-like the sun colour), which works well together. The yellow, in particular, really pops, which draws you in even more. 

## **Part 8: the Horned Rat — the Keep**
**Sam:** While The Tower may have told a sinister tale of the rise of the Skaven, The Keep is focused on the forces of Nurgle in Brass Keep chasing away a doomed assault by Clan Mange. This theme is conveyed by a number of images, including the discarded shields reminiscent of a Nurgle symbol and various weapons thrown on the banks of a rather bloody river, in particular, the spears arranged in the symbol of the Skaven. Seven is Nurgle’s sacred number, so we have seven rot flies defending the Keep or descending from the night sky. 

Centralised compositions like this often come together reasonably easily, and I was happy that the towers on both covers were quite distinct and central to the covers. Brass Keep had to look intimidating, obviously inhabited by the forces of Chaos, but also fitting within this specific inworld style, which gave me some flexibility in how exactly to depict it. Approvals came through, and so it was time to move into colour!

**DEVELOPER DIARY** 

As with all the pairs of Collector’s Edition covers, the main book and the companion needed to have one unifying colour (aside, of course, from the black and silver that are a feature on every Collector’s Edition cover), and one colour of its own. We chose green as the unifying colour, and then paired that with a rich, bloody red. Of course, the deep river had to be red, which pretty much fixed the rats fleeing as being green to act in stark contrast. Vibrant warm red as a primary colour is complemented by the secondary colour cool green. The Keep is green with silver and red to accent it and ensure it wasn’t just a series of blocks of the same colour. The placement of colours was approved, and that meant I could move on to my final stage here. 

And again, as you can see in the image above, this stage did not include too many changes. The image took shape as the linework was removed and the blocks of colour refined, the Keep took a bit of a battering as I carved some black into the green to show weathering and damage. In the end I thought it properly depicted enough of a story of a collision of sides, critical in ensuring it ended up being more than just ‘here’s a tower’ and instead suggested a meaningful setting with a dramatic and violent backstory. 

With the artwork so far approved, my part of the Collector’s Edition covers of **The Horned Rat** and **the Horned Rat Companion** was complete, and as always, I handed my work over to Rachael to work her magic before the big reveal! 

**Rachael:** Using the first cover as a striking template, Sam added a lot of detail to this cover as well. By this stage, we really knew the direction we wanted to take. The only detail I changed on ‘The Keep’ was the horns; they resembled ork horns, so I needed to straighten them up. 

The river is one of the main features with the lines appearing to run off the page. Again, movement is key, so the deep river needed to look like it was flowing fast. The blood river is after all the blood of all the dead skaven that were massacred. I also wanted a rapid flow, to help the rats swim easily (though that wasn’t my first thought). 

For continuity with the Tower cover I wanted to add the same wood-carved finish to these rats as well. The rat on the left had so much character, I needed to tone it down a bit. Next, I added lighting and shadow detailing to the other elements, especially the weapons. Originally the spears were in colour, but blades are usually silver right? So let's make them silver on the cover to make them stand out. The weapons needed some texture, so I created the wood-grain effect on the club handles which are a great contrast to the sharp spikes. 

## **Developer Diary**
I brought the mountains down a fraction to emphasise the sheer scale of The Keep’s immense size. Adding the snow caps helped with that and also highlighted the freezing conditions, which made the scene even more hostile. 

The rot flies, said to be servants of Nurgle, sent to spread diseases needed strong wings, strong enough to carry any human on their back. So for some, I added lots of detail so that they appeared tough enough to hold them and their riders. Again movement worked well here, drawing your eye up to the eerie night sky. Whether it’s the fleeing rats swimming towards you or the rot flies flying at an unnerving pace, I think Sam and I created a sinister image that will leave a remarkable impact.
